properties.nom: Chambly: birth of Étienne Provost
properties.description: Étienne Provost is born in Chambly, on the Richelieu River, on December 21, 1785. He is the first child of Albert Provost's third marriage, to Marie-Anne Mainard (Ménard); Albert was a prosperous farmer and father of some fifteen children. The baptismal record, written the same day by the parish priest Ménard, names as godfather Étienne Frichet, who signs, and as godmother Thérèse Laroque, widow Mainard, who declares she cannot sign. His father, Albert, son of Gabriel Provost and Marie-Anne Bourassa, married three times at Chambly (Marie-Louise Paquet in 1770, eight children; Magdeleine Lebeau in 1783; Marie-Anne Mainard in 1785), so Étienne grows up among six older half-siblings and five younger brothers. Albert is buried at Chambly on March 5, 1796, aged 46: Étienne is ten, and he will never learn to read or write. Almost nothing is known of his youth; he is not yet twenty, writes Denis Vaugeois, when he chooses the fur trade and the Far West, with St. Louis as his base.
properties.sources: Register of Saint-Joseph parish, Chambly, baptisms of 1785, f. 39, entry of December 21, 1785 (photograph at the Chambly presbytery, Etienne_Provost.jpg in the author's Drive) ; Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Bouchard, Serge and Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. De remarquables oubliés, vol. 2, Montreal, Lux, ch. “Hommes des montagnes: Provost, Chalifoux, Robidoux” (epub in the author's Drive); Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Étienne Provost et le Grand Lac Salé”, entry in the series De remarquables oubliés (Serge Bouchard), document in the author's Drive (etienne_provost.pdf) ; Drouin, Quebec, Canada, Vital and Church Records (Drouin Collection), 1621-1968, Saint-Joseph parish, Chambly (Ancestry, accessed November 20, 2026): marriages of 1770, 1783 and 1785, baptisms 1771-1792, burial of Albert Provost on March 5, 1796
properties.note: Exact day from Vaugeois; Tykal and Hafen give only 1785. The Utah State Historical Society photo collection suggests 1782. Point at the Saint-Joseph church in Chambly. The full family, with each record, is in the Ancestry tree and in the “Family tree” tab of the reading room.

registres.legende: Baptism of Étienne, son of Albert Provost and Marie-Anne Mainard, Chambly, December 21, 1785 (right-hand page, bottom); godfather Étienne Frichet, godmother Thérèse Laroque, widow Mainard; signed Mennard, parish priest

properties.nom: Quebec City: the ancestor Martin Prévost and Marie-Olivier Manitouabeouich (1644)
properties.description: Vaugeois links Étienne to Martin Prévost, the first of the name in New France, who married Marie-Olivier Sylvestre Manitouabeouich in Quebec City in 1644. She was Champlain's adopted daughter, from a Huron-Wendat and Algonquin family: one of the very first French-Indigenous marriages solemnized in the colony.
properties.sources: Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON)
properties.note: Genealogical entry, outside Étienne's lifetime: it appears from the start of the timeline. The detailed line of descent from Martin to Étienne has yet to be established in the parish registers.

properties.nom: St. Louis: a Canadien in the capital of the fur trade
properties.description: Provost makes St. Louis his base for some thirty-five years, between campaigns in the West. He arrives there by 1814-1815 at the latest, in a town still largely French-speaking and dominated by the Chouteaus, Prattes and Bertholds, for whom he will work.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Étienne Provost et le Grand Lac Salé”, entry in the series De remarquables oubliés (Serge Bouchard), document in the author's Drive (etienne_provost.pdf); Gitlin, Jay (2010), The Bourgeois Frontier: French Towns, French Traders, and American Expansion, New Haven, Yale University Press, PDF p. 139 (author's Drive) ; press: Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026
properties.note: The De remarquables oubliés sheet dates his arrival to 1815; Tykal has him leaving for the Arkansas as early as 1814. Point on the riverfront of the old town.

presse.legende: Missouri Republican, 8 nov. 1827 : lettre en souffrance pour « Etienne Proveau »

properties.nom: Upper Arkansas: the Joseph Philibert expedition (1814)
properties.description: In 1814, Provost belongs to the brigade of Joseph Philibert, a Montrealer settled in St. Louis. The brigade numbers eighteen Canadiens and joins Ezekiel Williams's party on the Arkansas; Williams's journal names Provost, Pierre Lespérance, Joseph Bissonnette dit Bijou, François Leclerc, Joseph Livernois, Charles Beaubien, Duchesne, Grenier, Lalande, Ledoux, Leroux and Nolan. In September, at Taos, they are arrested, jailed in Santa Fe and expelled without their goods. Philibert returns to St. Louis, leaving nine men, Provost among them, to hunt in the mountains.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Bouchard, Serge and Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. De remarquables oubliés, vol. 2, Montreal, Lux, ch. “Hommes des montagnes: Provost, Chalifoux, Robidoux” (epub in the author's Drive)
properties.note: Schematic point on the upper Arkansas (near present-day Pueblo). The 1814-1815 imprisonment is known only from Tykal; Philibert's men later pass into the service of Chouteau and De Mun.

properties.nom: Huerfano: the missed rendezvous of 1815
properties.description: Philibert had arranged to meet his nine men in 1815 at the Huerfano, near the Purgatoire. He returns with Auguste-Pierre Chouteau and Jules de Mun, to whom he sells his company along the way, but does not find them: starving, they had taken refuge in Taos months earlier. Chouteau and De Mun keep this core of men in the mountains; Provost's party is attacked by the Arapaho.
properties.sources: Bouchard, Serge and Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. De remarquables oubliés, vol. 2, Montreal, Lux, ch. “Hommes des montagnes: Provost, Chalifoux, Robidoux” (epub in the author's Drive)
properties.note: Point at Huerfano Butte (Colorado), schematic.

properties.nom: Taos: Chouteau and De Mun in Spanish territory (1816)
properties.description: Leaving St. Louis in September 1815, Auguste-Pierre Chouteau and Jules de Mun go up to trap on the upper Arkansas with some forty men, including Provost. At first they obtain permission from the Spanish authorities to hunt, notably around Taos.
properties.sources: Roy, Alain, “Sur la piste de Santa Fe, 1721-1880”, in Frenette, Yves, Étienne Rivard and Marc St-Hilaire (ed.) (2012), La francophonie nord-américaine, Québec, PUL, series “Atlas historique du Québec”, p. 103; Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org)
properties.note: Point at Taos.

properties.nom: Chouteau's Island: refuge on the Arkansas
properties.description: On the way back, the party of Chouteau, Provost and De Mun is attacked and entrenches itself on an island in the Arkansas, since renamed Chouteau's Island. The spot becomes a landmark on the future Santa Fe Trail.
properties.sources: Roy, Alain, “Sur la piste de Santa Fe, 1721-1880”, in Frenette, Yves, Étienne Rivard and Marc St-Hilaire (ed.) (2012), La francophonie nord-américaine, Québec, PUL, series “Atlas historique du Québec”, p. 103
properties.note: The island has disappeared as the riverbed shifted; point near present-day Lakin (Kansas).

properties.nom: Santa Fe: “Ettinne Provott” in prison (1817)
properties.description: In May 1817, the party is arrested by Spanish soldiers, who accuse it of hunting and trading on their territory. The men are taken to Santa Fe and locked up for several weeks; their furs and goods, worth $30,000 according to De Mun, are confiscated. The twenty-one Canadiens remain captive for forty-eight days; the list in the Santa Fe military archives includes Toussaint Charbonneau, the former guide of Lewis and Clark. “Ettinne Provott” signs the prisoners' declaration before being released and sent back to the United States.
properties.sources: Old Santa Fe: A Magazine of History, Archaeology, Genealogy and Biography, vol. 1, Santa Fe, 1913-1914, p. 375 (archive.org); Roy, Alain, “Sur la piste de Santa Fe, 1721-1880”, in Frenette, Yves, Étienne Rivard and Marc St-Hilaire (ed.) (2012), La francophonie nord-américaine, Québec, PUL, series “Atlas historique du Québec”, p. 103; Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Bouchard, Serge and Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. De remarquables oubliés, vol. 2, Montreal, Lux, ch. “Hommes des montagnes: Provost, Chalifoux, Robidoux” (epub in the author's Drive)
properties.note: Amount and length of detention from the complaint of Chouteau and De Mun, as summarized by the Atlas historique du Québec and Old Santa Fe. Point at the Palace of the Governors.

properties.nom: Taos: the return, just after Mexican independence
properties.description: Drawing on what he has learned of the country, Provost returns to New Mexico around 1822, as soon as independent Mexico opens the Santa Fe trade. Taos becomes his base: there he meets Antoine Robidoux, with whom he will later work in the Uinta country.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Nelson, Jack William (2003), Forgotten Pathfinders Along the North Branch of the Old Spanish Trail, 1650-1850, PDF p. 41 (author's Drive); “Etienne Provost”, historytogo.utah.gov (Utah State Historical Society), accessed November 2026
properties.note: Vaugeois dates the return to 1821, Nelson to 1823. The De remarquables oubliés sheet credits him with founding the Rocky Mountain Fur Company in 1822: this is a confusion with the enterprise of Ashley and Henry, to which Provost never belonged.

properties.nom: Taos: “Provoe & Leclere” (letter of Céran St. Vrain, April 21, 1824)
properties.description: Having reached Taos in March 1824, Céran St. Vrain writes to Bernard Pratte on April 21 that business is bad, but that he expects to sell his goods to “Provoe & Leclere” when they return from their hunt. This is the first written trace of Provost's partnership with François Leclerc.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R. (1954), “When Was Bent's Fort Built?”, The Colorado Magazine, vol. 31, no. 2, p. 107-108; letter published by Dale L. Morgan, Provo, Pioneer Mormon City (1942), p. 24-25
properties.note: The identification of Leclerc (François?) is proposed by Hafen.

properties.nom: Uinta Basin: the hunt of Provost and Leclerc (1824)
properties.description: As partners, Provost and Leclerc leave Taos by the north branch of the Old Spanish Trail to trap the Uinta Basin and the Green River. After the October massacre, Provost spends the winter of 1824-1825 in the region of the White and Green rivers.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Nelson, Jack William (1996), “The North Branch of the “Old Spanish Trail””, Journal of the Western Slope, vol. 11, no. 4, PDF p. 37 (author's Drive); Dale, Harrison C. (1918), The Ashley-Smith Explorations and the Discovery of a Central Route to the Pacific, 1822-1829, Cleveland, Arthur H. Clark, p. 94-95, 103 (archive.org)
properties.note: Point at the confluence of the White and the Green (present-day Ouray, Utah).

properties.nom: Jordan River: the Bad Gocha massacre (October 1824)
properties.description: In October 1824, the party camps near Utah Lake, probably on the Jordan. A Shoshone chief whom the whites call “Bad Gocha” offers to smoke the pipe, on condition that no weapons or metal objects be within reach. The trappers lay down their rifles; at a signal, the Shoshone draw hidden knives. Provost escapes with two to four companions through the Wasatch Mountains, toward the northeast.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Etienne Provost”, historytogo.utah.gov (Utah State Historical Society), accessed November 2026; Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Chittenden, Hiram Martin (1902), The American Fur Trade of the Far West, New York, Francis P. Harper, vol. 1, p. 261-280 (archive.org); Harris, W. R. (1909), The Catholic Church in Utah, Salt Lake City, Intermountain Catholic Press, p. 259-262 (archive.org) ; press: Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026
properties.note: The number of dead varies by source: eight (Tykal), eight to ten (Vaugeois), fifteen (Nelson 1996), seventeen (Harris). So does the place: the Jordan near the Great Salt Lake (Tykal), the mouth of the Provo (Harris). Peter Skene Ogden would learn in 1825 that Alexander Ross's party had earlier robbed and killed Shoshone, which would explain this revenge.

presse.legende: Deseret News, 24 juillet 1912 : « The Coming of Provot »
Idaho State Journal, 8 déc. 1955 : la bande dessinée Dan'l Hale

properties.nom: Great Salt Lake: “the first white man”? (1824)
properties.description: Provost is said to be the first white man to have seen the Great Salt Lake, in the fall of 1824, a few weeks before Jim Bridger, who is traditionally credited with the discovery (winter 1824-1825). The evidence is indirect but consistent.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Etienne Provost”, historytogo.utah.gov (Utah State Historical Society), accessed November 2026; Dolin, Eric Jay (2010), Fur, Fortune, and Empire: The Epic History of the Fur Trade in America, New York, W. W. Norton, PDF p. note 47 (author's Drive); Dale, Harrison C. (1918), The Ashley-Smith Explorations and the Discovery of a Central Route to the Pacific, 1822-1829, Cleveland, Arthur H. Clark, p. 94-95, 103 (archive.org)
properties.note: Disputed discovery: Bancroft even suggests a visit before 1824, without proof. Schematic point on the east shore of the lake.

properties.nom: Utah Lake: temporary trading posts (1824-1825)
properties.description: Having survived the massacre, Provost sets up temporary trading posts on the shores of Utah Lake and the Great Salt Lake. The river that flows into Utah Lake, and later the town founded on its banks, will bear his name.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Étienne Provost et le Grand Lac Salé”, entry in the series De remarquables oubliés (Serge Bouchard), document in the author's Drive (etienne_provost.pdf); Chittenden, Hiram Martin (1902), The American Fur Trade of the Far West, New York, Francis P. Harper, vol. 2-3, p. 626, 796 (archive.org)
properties.note: Locations unknown. The De remarquables oubliés sheet speaks of eight posts, a figure the biographers do not repeat.

properties.nom: Mountain Green (Weber Canyon): Ogden against the Americans (May 1825)
properties.description: In May 1825, in Weber Canyon, Provost meets the Hudson's Bay Company brigade led by Peter Skene Ogden and witnesses the clash between Ogden and Johnson Gardner, Ashley's lieutenant, who urges Ogden's engagés to desert. An irony noted by Tykal: of all the men present, only Provost, who had come from Taos under a Mexican license, had the right to hunt in this territory, which was still Mexican.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Etienne Provost”, historytogo.utah.gov (Utah State Historical Society), accessed November 2026; Dale, Harrison C. (1918), The Ashley-Smith Explorations and the Discovery of a Central Route to the Pacific, 1822-1829, Cleveland, Arthur H. Clark, p. 94-95, 103 (archive.org)
properties.note: Point at Mountain Green (Utah).

properties.nom: Fruitland: Provost meets William Ashley (June 1825)
properties.description: After a disastrous descent of the Green River in bullboats, William H. Ashley comes upon some of Provost's trappers, who take him to their camp. In June 1825, near present-day Fruitland, Provost agrees to guide him by the Duchesne and Strawberry Creek, then north to the site of the first rendezvous. He does not, however, become one of Ashley's employees.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Nelson, Jack William (2003), Forgotten Pathfinders Along the North Branch of the Old Spanish Trail, 1650-1850, PDF p. 40 (author's Drive); Nichols, Jeffrey D. (1995), “Fellow Trappers Called Etienne Provost “The Man of the Mountains””, History Blazer, Utah State Historical Society, August 1995 (historytogo.utah.gov); Contributions to the Historical Society of Montana, vol. 9 (1923), p. 324-325
properties.note: Dellenbaugh (1902) and Dale (1918) also report a Provost camp at Brown's Hole, well stocked with food and horses when Ashley's starving men arrived; Dale considers this account doubtful.

properties.nom: Henry's Fork: the first Rocky Mountain rendezvous (July 1825)
properties.description: Guided by Provost, Ashley reaches Henry's Fork of the Green River, where the first annual trappers' rendezvous is held in early July 1825: Ashley trades his goods there for the furs of hunters scattered through the mountains. The Canadiens present look to Provost as their natural guide.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Nichols, Jeffrey D. (1995), “Fellow Trappers Called Etienne Provost “The Man of the Mountains””, History Blazer, Utah State Historical Society, August 1995 (historytogo.utah.gov); Hebard, Grace Raymond and E. A. Brininstool (1922), The Bozeman Trail, vol. 1, p. 38
properties.note: Point near Burntfork (Wyoming).

properties.nom: South Pass: a discovery attributed to Provost
properties.description: Several early writers credit Provost with discovering South Pass, the easy crossing of the Rockies later followed by emigrants bound for Oregon and California: the Annals of Wyoming date it to 1822, Chittenden and Harris to 1823, Bartlett to 1824. Historians today accept the “rediscovery” of the pass by Jedediah Smith and Thomas Fitzpatrick in the spring of 1824, on the advice of the Crow.
properties.sources: Annals of Wyoming, vol. 1 (1923), p. 756; Chittenden, Hiram Martin (1902), The American Fur Trade of the Far West, New York, Francis P. Harper, vol. 1, p. 261-280 (archive.org); Harris, W. R. (1909), The Catholic Church in Utah, Salt Lake City, Intermountain Catholic Press, p. 259-262 (archive.org); Bartlett, I. S. (ed.) (1918), History of Wyoming, vol. 1, p. 478; “Étienne Provost et le Grand Lac Salé”, entry in the series De remarquables oubliés (Serge Bouchard), document in the author's Drive (etienne_provost.pdf) ; press: Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026
properties.note: Traditional attribution, unproven; no contemporary source places Provost at the pass.

presse.legende: Nebraska City Weekly, 24 juin 1902 : la tradition attribue le col du Sud à Provost
Salt Lake Herald, 25 déc. 1904 : le parti de Provost, 1823

properties.nom: Utah Lake: did Provost resupply Jedediah Smith's men?
properties.description: Bancroft reports that a party led by Provost fed Jedediah Smith's starving men and gave them fresh horses near Utah Lake.
properties.sources: Bancroft, Hubert Howe (1889), History of Utah, 1540-1886, San Francisco, The History Company, p. 22, n. 4 (archive.org)
properties.note: Isolated episode of uncertain date; to be checked in Morgan (1953).

properties.nom: Fort Lookout: down the Missouri (1826)
properties.description: After the 1826 rendezvous, where Jim Beckwourth places him, though not with certainty, Provost heads back to the United States by the Missouri; Hafen's biographical sketch records him at Fort Lookout, a post in the Missouri valley.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. Clark, vol. 6 (1968), p. 371-386; mentioned p. 376; Hafen, LeRoy R. (1968), “Etienne Provost, Mountain Man and Utah Pioneer”, Utah Historical Quarterly, vol. 36, no. 2
properties.note: Point at Fort Lookout (South Dakota).

properties.nom: St. Louis: “the soul of the hunters in the mountains” (September 1826)
properties.description: In September 1826, Provost is back in St. Louis and trading with B. Pratte & Company. Barthélemy Berthold, a partner in the firm, writes that year that he is “the soul of the hunters in the mountains.” He enters the service of Astor's American Fur Company, whose Western Department is the Pratte-Chouteau firm.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R. (1968), “Etienne Provost, Mountain Man and Utah Pioneer”, Utah Historical Quarterly, vol. 36, no. 2; Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org)
properties.note: Point near the levee, where the Chouteau and Pratte warehouses stood.

properties.nom: St. Louis: the tavern and the grocery
properties.description: From about 1827, between his seasons in the West, Provost keeps a tavern and a grocery in St. Louis. According to Vaugeois, he is in partnership with his brother-in-law Clément Salle dit Lajoie. A bon vivant, he is famous for his love of good food and drink.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Gitlin, Jay (2010), The Bourgeois Frontier: French Towns, French Traders, and American Expansion, New Haven, Yale University Press, PDF p. 139 (author's Drive); research by O. J. Caron for the Aubry Atlas (2026), added to the atlas “Les Canadiens français de l'Ouest” (entries PV-01 to PV-05) ; press: Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026
properties.note: Address unknown; point in the Second Street Frenchtown, where Havard places Provost. The 1845 directory lists a “Clement Lambert, coffee-house” at the corner of Second and Lombard streets (see L36).

presse.legende: Missouri Republican, 1er mai 1834 : licences de « Provost, Etien », marchand et tavernier

properties.nom: Fort Floyd (later Fort Union): McKenzie sends Provost to find the free trappers (fall 1828)
properties.description: In the fall of 1828, Kenneth McKenzie, charged by Astor with opening the Rocky Mountain trade, sends Provost, “a former Ashley man,” into the mountains to tell the free trappers that the American Fur Company will buy their furs at a good price. Provost brings Rocky Mountain Fur Company trappers back to the post at the mouth of the Yellowstone.
properties.sources: Dolin, Eric Jay (2010), Fur, Fortune, and Empire: The Epic History of the Fur Trade in America, New York, W. W. Norton, PDF p. 325 (author's Drive); Chittenden, Hiram Martin (1902), The American Fur Trade of the Far West, New York, Francis P. Harper, vol. 1, p. 305-306, 328 (archive.org); Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. Clark, vol. 6 (1968), p. 371-386; mentioned p. 377
properties.note: Fort Floyd was renamed Fort Union around 1830.

properties.nom: Crow country: the first wife and the son Nicolas (hypothesis)
properties.description: Before his marriage in St. Louis, Provost is said to have had a son named Nicolas with an Indigenous woman, a Crow according to family tradition; Bouchard and Lévesque place this union in the winter of 1828. A grandson, Michel, is said to have been born in Canada.
properties.sources: Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Bouchard, Serge and Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. De remarquables oubliés, vol. 2, Montreal, Lux, ch. “Hommes des montagnes: Provost, Chalifoux, Robidoux” (epub in the author's Drive); “Étienne Provost et le Grand Lac Salé”, entry in the series De remarquables oubliés (Serge Bouchard), document in the author's Drive (etienne_provost.pdf)
properties.note: Union attested only by the tradition reported by Vaugeois and De remarquables oubliés; date and place unknown. The atlas places the point in Crow country (Bighorn-Yellowstone), where the free trappers sought in 1828-1829 roamed.

properties.nom: St. Louis: marriage to Marie-Rose Lambert, daughter of Lambert Salé dit Lajoie (August 4, 1829)
properties.description: Back in St. Louis on July 27, 1829, Provost learns that Marie-Rose Lambert, daughter of his partner Lambert Salé dit Lajoie and of Madeleine Delor, twelve years his junior, has been a widow since the fall; he has known her since at least 1826. The wedding is set for August 4 and blessed by the Jesuit Joseph Anthony Lutz. The record, which Provost signs with a cross, calls the bride “daughter of Lambert Salé, dit Lajoy, and Magdeleine Delor”; among the witnesses her father (“Lajoye”) and her brother Clément Lambert sign, Marie Ménard makes her mark, and “Mr J. Laberge” is probably Joseph-Marie La Barge, father of the future pilot. For the wedding Provost buys blankets, cassinette, scarlet cloth and silver lace. The marriage also has a business side: from the summer of 1829 Marie-Rose appears as a creditor in the company's books.
properties.sources: Havard, Gilles (2019), L'Amérique fantôme. Les aventuriers francophones du Nouveau Monde, Paris, Flammarion, ch. 8 « L'homme des montagnes : Étienne Provost », p. 323-379 (PDF du Drive de l'auteur, dossier GILLES_HAVARD, lu intégralement le 19 nov. 2026), p. 339-340 ; Tykal, Jack B., « Provost, Etienne », Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copie du Drive de l'auteur, t_000690.pdf ; uen.org) ; Vaugeois, Denis, « Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques », Le Devoir, 16-17 février 2002 (coupure du Drive de l'auteur, dossier ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON) ; Bouchard, Serge et Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. properties.nom: St. Louis: birth of Mary Rose, “daughter of Étienne Provo” (May 1, 1830)
properties.description: The death certificate of Mary Rose Pillsbury (1913) states that she was born in St. Louis on May 1, 1830, the daughter of “Etienne Provo,” born in Canada. The date falls one year after the marriage: she would be the couple's only known daughter, whom Audubon sees aboard the steamboat in 1843.

properties.note: The certificate names the mother “Madelin Delor,” born in St. Louis. She is not Mary Rose's mother but her maternal grandmother: the 1829 marriage record calls Marie-Rose “daughter of Lambert Salé, dit Lajoy, and Magdeleine Delor.” The 1913 informant, Charles G. Grimm, husband of the deceased's granddaughter, skipped a generation (see the “Family tree” tab of the reading room). The censuses confirm the line: in 1860 Mary Rose lives with her husband James A. H. Pillsbury and their daughter Mary Frances; in 1900 and 1910 she lives with her daughter and son-in-law Charles G. Grimm. No baptism was found in the Drouin index for St. Louis. Schematic point in the old town.

properties.nom: Fort Union: hunter and boatman for the company (1830-1831)
properties.description: In 1830, Provost is among the hunters at Fort Union; in 1831, the American Fur Company roll lists him as a boatman. The fort, built by McKenzie at the confluence of the Yellowstone and the Missouri, becomes the hub of the upper Missouri trade.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. Clark, vol. 6 (1968), p. 371-386; mentioned p. 378-379

properties.nom: Bayou Salade: guide to Fontenelle and Drips (1834)
properties.description: In the spring of 1834, Provost guides Lucien Fontenelle and Andrew Drips, American Fur Company brigade leaders, to the Bayou Salade (South Park, Colorado), a vast high-altitude park rich in game.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. Clark, vol. 6 (1968), p. 371-386; mentioned p. 379
properties.note: Hafen dates the episode to 1833-1834; the 1834 date follows Hafen's biographical summary as reproduced by Prabook.

properties.nom: Ham's Fork: the 1834 rendezvous
properties.description: In July 1834, Provost leads an American Fur Company party to the rendezvous on Ham's Fork, a tributary of Black's Fork (Green River). Until 1838 he escorts the company's caravans to the annual rendezvous in this way. The traveler William Marshall Anderson, whom he guides in 1834, remembers his orders in French, “Fumez la pipe!” (smoke the pipe) for a halt, “Gardez aux rames!” (mind the oars), and bids him farewell at the end of his journal.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. presse.legende: Missouri Republican, 26 août 1834 : « From the Mountains »

properties.nom: Bellevue: the fur barge (1834)
properties.description: At the end of the 1834 season, Provost takes the barge carrying the company's furs down the Missouri to the Bellevue post, kept by Lucien Fontenelle and later Peter Sarpy, on its way to St. Louis.
properties.sources: Chittenden, Hiram Martin (1902), The American Fur Trade of the Far West, New York, Francis P. properties.note: Point at Bellevue (Nebraska).

properties.nom: Fort William (Laramie): with the caravans of 1836
properties.description: In 1836, Provost passes through Fort William, on the Laramie, which the American Fur Company has just bought, with the caravan going up from Liberty (Missouri) and the Council Bluffs post toward the rendezvous.
properties.sources: Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. Clark, vol. 6 (1968), p. 371-386; mentioned p. 381
properties.note: Point at Fort Laramie (Wyoming).

properties.nom: Horse Creek (Green River): Alfred Jacob Miller paints “Proveau” (1837 rendezvous)
properties.description: In the spring of 1837, Provost is the sub-leader of the American Fur Company supply caravan led by Thomas Fitzpatrick, which leaves from near Westport. The painter Alfred Jacob Miller travels with it, hired by the Scottish captain William Drummond Stewart. Miller paints “Monsieur Proveau” at least three times: in Attrapez des Chevaux (c. 1855) and Catching Up (1858-1860), standing in front of his tent with his hands cupped around his mouth, calling the men to catch their horses; and in Threatened Attack, the caravan facing a party of Lakota. In his notes, Miller calls him a “subleader, with a corpus round as a porpoise”, “adipose & rotonde”, “larding the lean earth as he walks along” (a Shakespeare line about Falstaff), with “stentorian lungs”. See the “Le témoin Miller” tab in the reading room.
properties.sources: Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? Des liens historiques et généalogiques”, Le Devoir, 16-17 February 2002 (clipping in the author's Drive, folder ETIENNE_PROVOST_AUDUBON); Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Bouchard, Serge and Marie-Christine Lévesque (2014), Ils ont couru l'Amérique. Hardee, “A Corpus Round as a Porpoise…”, alfredjacobmiller.com (accessed 21 Nov. 2026)
properties.note: Point at the confluence of Horse Creek and the Green River (near Daniel, Wyoming).

properties.nom: St. Louis: Provost brings news of the smallpox epidemic (February 24, 1838)
properties.description: On February 24, 1838, Provost reaches St. Louis from the upper country, late in the season. He brings news of the smallpox epidemic that has been ravaging the nations of the upper Missouri (Mandan, Arikara, Assiniboine, Blackfoot) since the summer of 1837; the company had sent him to assess its extent. In the spring of 1838 he attends his last rendezvous and will never return to the Rockies.
properties.sources: Chittenden, Hiram Martin (1902), The American Fur Trade of the Far West, New York, Francis P. Harper, vol. 2-3, p. 626 (archive.org); Harris, W. R. properties.nom: Fort Pierre: head of Nicollet and Frémont's men (July 1-3, 1839)
properties.description: In 1839, the American Fur Company lends Provost to Joseph-Nicolas Nicollet, who is mapping the plateaus between the Missouri and the upper Mississippi with the young John C. Frémont. Nicollet writes that he brought from St. Louis five men who “were certainly worth ten,” including “Étienne Provost, known as the man of the mountains,” whom he promotes to head of his men. On July 1, Provost comes to report that the outfit is ready; the caravan, nineteen people, ten carts and thirty horses, crosses the swollen Missouri on July 1 and 2 and climbs onto the Coteau du Missouri on the 3rd.
properties.sources: Nicollet, Joseph-Nicolas (1841), Report Intended to Illustrate a Map of the Hydrographical Basin of the Upper Mississippi River, Senate, 26th Congress, 2nd session, doc. 237, p. 42-50 (author's Drive); Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); “Etienne Provost”, historytogo.utah.gov (Utah State Historical Society), accessed November 2026; Hafen, LeRoy R., “Etienne Provost”, in Hafen (ed.), The Mountain Men and the Fur Trade of the Far West, Glendale, Arthur H. Clark, vol. 6 (1968), p. 371-386; mentioned p. 382
properties.note: Point at Fort Pierre.

properties.nom: Devils Lake: end of the Nicollet expedition (July 29-August 7, 1839)
properties.description: By way of the Coteau du Missouri and the Rivière à Jacques (James River), the convoy reaches Devils Lake (Mini-wakan) on July 29, 1839. It stays nine days, near a camp just vacated by the Red River Métis, before heading back to the southeast.
properties.sources: Nicollet, Joseph-Nicolas (1841), Report Intended to Illustrate a Map of the Hydrographical Basin of the Upper Mississippi River, Senate, 26th Congress, 2nd session, doc. 237, p. 42-50 (author's Drive); Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org)
properties.note: Point at Devils Lake (North Dakota).

properties.nom: St. Louis: recruiter and escort for the American Fur Company (1839-1849)
properties.description: From 1839 until his death, Provost recruits the company's new engagés every winter and takes them to their Missouri posts in the spring. The company also hires out his services as a guide to private expeditions: British officers garrisoned in Montreal, whom he takes buffalo hunting as far as the plains of Texas in 1840; Audubon in 1843; and in 1844 the party of the Count of Otranto, son of Napoleon's Minister of Police, no doubt his most demanding client.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B., “Provost, Etienne”, Utah History Encyclopedia, Salt Lake City, University of Utah Press, 1994 (copy in the author's Drive, t_000690.pdf; uen.org); Vaugeois, Denis, “Provost, Québec - Provo, Salt Lake, Utah ? properties.nom: St. Louis: the Second Street Frenchtown
properties.description: Gilles Havard places Provost in Frenchtown, south of the Old Cathedral (Second and Third streets, between Poplar and Lombard), based on the 1847 directory and the 1845 municipal census. The 1840-1841 and 1845 directories list an “H. N. Provost,” grocer, at the southwest corner of Second and Lombard, across from Clément Lambert's coffee-house; but the 1851 directory still lists a “Henry N. Provost, mountain trader”: no doubt a relative.

properties.nom: Fort Union: old Provost, Audubon's hunter (June-August 1843)
properties.description: Arriving at Fort Union on June 12, 1843, with Audubon aboard the steamboat Omega, “old” Provost, who has brought his daughter, leads the expedition's hunters: he sets out before dawn across the Missouri, brings back deer and antelope, prepares the brine for the skins, carries messages to the rival fort and makes calls that imitate the bleating of fawns. Audubon admires the skill of his Canadien hunters, Bonaventure Le Brun, Charles Primeau and Alexis Bombardier, and notes down their Canadianisms.

properties.nom: St. Charles: “old Provost” walks home (October 18, 1843)
properties.description: On the way back, at St. Charles, Audubon notes that Provost, thoroughly drunk, set off on foot for St. Louis, where his wife, his daughter and his brother-in-law Clément Salle dit Lajoie await him. For nearly five months of service, this “very respectable man” receives $214 from Audubon and $78.33 from the Upper Missouri Outfit.

properties.nom: Fort Pierre: the last trips up the Missouri (1845-1849)
properties.description: Until the end of the 1840s, Provost goes up the Missouri every spring to the company's posts; Vaugeois says he was still active as a guide between Fort Pierre and St. Louis. His last journey to the upper country, in 1848 or 1849, is aboard the steamboat of his friend Captain Joseph LaBarge; LaBarge and Henri Picotte will keep his legend alive.

properties.nom: St. Louis: death and burial (July 3-4, 1850)
properties.description: Back in his house on Lombard Street in 1849, Étienne Provost dies suddenly, of a heart attack according to Bouchard and Lévesque, in St. Louis on July 3, 1850, aged 64, without knowing that the Mormons have just given his name to a town in Utah. He is buried the next day from the Old Cathedral, whose register records him as the husband of “Maria Rose Lombard.”

properties.nom: Provo River: the “Provost Fork” on Frémont's maps (1845)
properties.description: The account of Frémont's expedition published in 1845, for which Kit Carson served as guide, names the river flowing down to Utah Lake “Provost Fork.” The trapper's name is thus printed on maps before the Mormons arrive; the Jordan was also called Proveau's Fork.

properties.nom: Provo: the town bears Provost's name, shortened (1849)
properties.description: In the spring of 1849, some thirty Mormon families led by John S. Higbee build Fort Utah on the river of Utah Valley. The trapper Barney Ward tells them it is also called the Provo, after Provost; in October 1849, the Church conference orders the founding of the town of Provo there. Provost left behind, Vaugeois notes, the last two letters of his name.

properties.nom: St. Louis: death of Mary Rose Pillsbury, Provost's daughter (1913)
properties.description: Mary Rose Pillsbury, a widow, probably of James A. Pillsbury, dies aged 83 at 4231 South 37th Street; she is buried in Calvary Cemetery on August 11, 1913. Her death certificate names her as the daughter of “Etienne Provo,” born in Canada. The death notice in the St. Louis Star and Times names her as the mother of Mrs. Chas. G. Grimm and of a son named Etienne Pillsbury (after his grandfather), and grandmother of a nun of the Good Shepherd convent (probably one of the four Grimm daughters listed in 1900 and 1910: Mary E., Clara E., Margaret M. A. or Agnes Maria); the funeral left on Monday, August 11, from her home at 4221 South Thirty-seventh for St. Thomas of Aquin church, then Calvary Cemetery.

properties.description: In Le Devoir, the historian and publisher Denis Vaugeois tells Provost's life story, from the Richelieu to the Great Salt Lake, and is amused that the Mormon city keeps the name of a jovial Catholic tavern keeper whose first union was with an Indigenous woman.

properties.description: The Quebec novelist Louis Hamelin turns Audubon's 1843 journey up the Missouri into a sweeping novel, in which Étienne Provost serves as guide and as a counterpoint to the naturalist.

properties.nom: St. Louis: the house at the corner of Lombard and Second streets (1843-1850)
properties.description: City tax lists place Provost's lots in the First Ward: a lot on Third Street as early as 1831, then lots in blocks 49 (Lombard Street) and 76 (Cedar Street), next to the Cailloux, Dufresne, Papin and Hernandez families. On May 18, 1835, Etienne Provot and Marie Rose, his wife, sold half of a lot in block 76 to Sarah Ann Langley. The 1850 death notice confirms he lived “on the corner of Lombard and Second streets”.

properties.nom: Lee County, Iowa: Provost among the claimants of the Half-Breed Tract (1840-1852)
properties.description: On April 14, 1840, Josiah Spalding, Archibald Gamble, Patrick Walsh, “Etienne Prevost”, John B. Sarpy, Antoine Leclaire and others petitioned the Lee County district court to partition the “Half Breed tract”, 119,000 acres between the Mississippi and the Des Moines reserved in 1824 for Sauk and Fox Métis. Provost therefore held rights there, probably acquired as a creditor or through his family. In 1852, after his death, a sheriff's sale still executed a judgment in favour of the same claimants.
properties.sources: The Hawk-Eye and Iowa Patriot (Burlington), 2 juillet-10 sept. 1840 ; Democratic Banner (Davenport), 26 mars-19 nov. 1852 ; Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026.

properties.nom: Crow Creek: Provost awes the Yanktons (1847)
properties.description: On Joseph La Barge's first trip as master of his own steamboat, in 1847, the Yanktons at Crow Creek refused to let the crew load the wood cut for the boat and beat the deckhands with rawhides. According to the account published in 1903 by the South Dakota historical society, Etienne Provost, “a fearless frontiersman whom the Indians stood in awe of”, stepped in and the wood was loaded. That evening the attack resumed and a boatman was killed.
properties.sources: Minneapolis Journal, 7 sept. 1903, p. 11 (« Row with Redskins », dépêche de Pierre) ; repris par l'Argus-Leader et d'autres ; Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026.

properties.nom: Mandan village: the corn trick played on Audubon's scientist (1843)
properties.description: Joseph La Barge recalled that one of Audubon's assistants boasted he could name any plant from its leaf and stalk. Provost, then guiding the party, picked a young corn plant near a Mandan camp, showed only one leaf and let the scientist search his books in vain before revealing the kernel still at the root. The man became the laughing stock of the crew.
properties.sources: Récit syndiqué dans une vingtaine d'hebdos du Montana et de l'Utah, 25 déc. 1919-23 janv. 1920 (ex. Cascade Courier, 26 déc. 1919) ; Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026.
properties.note: Point at the Mandan villages near Fort Clark; the story gives no exact place.

properties.nom: Kansas City: Jim Bridger's monument recalls Provost's party (1904)
properties.description: In December 1904 the dedication of Jim Bridger's monument at Mount Washington Cemetery prompted articles in several major papers: in the fall of 1823 Ashley sent a new party under Etienne Provost, “a noted trapper and trader”, by the Bighorn and the Wind to the Green; Bridger was in it, and this party found South Pass.
properties.sources: St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 18 déc. 1904 ; Kansas City Star, 23 déc. 1904 ; Salt Lake Herald et Omaha Bee, 25 déc. 1904 ; Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026.

properties.nom: Salt Lake City: the Daughters of the American Revolution marker (1926)
properties.description: For the centennial of the first trappers' arrival, the Spirit of Liberty chapter of the DAR unveiled a monument with a marker honouring James Bridger, Jedediah Smith and Etienne Provot “at the new city park opposite St. Mark's hospital”. Mrs. George H. Dern, the governor's wife, unveiled it and J. Cecil Alter sketched the three men's lives.

properties.nom: Ogden: the alcove where Provost may have wintered (1824-1825)
properties.description: According to J. Cecil Alter, quoted by the Ogden Standard-Examiner in 1941, a sheltered alcove just north of present-day Ogden was the winter refuge of Etienne Provot and his men in 1824-25, then the winter quarters of Ashley's trappers in 1825-26 and the site of the 1826 rendezvous.
properties.sources: Ogden Standard-Examiner, 13 juillet 1941 (« Ogden Locale for Trapper Confabs »), repris en 1942 et 1946 ; Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026.
properties.note: Alter's hypothesis; most historians place Provost's winter near Utah Lake (L13). Schematic point north of Ogden.

properties.description: In 1960 the State Bank of Provo, founded in 1902, opened a modernist building whose lobby featured a contemporary statue of Etienne Provot, “the French Canadian trapper for whom the Provo River and the city of Provo were named”.
properties.sources: Salt Lake Tribune, 27 mai 1960 ; Newspapers.com (author's subscription), accessed November 20, 2026.
properties.note: Approximate position in downtown Provo; whether the statue survives is unknown.

properties.nom: Chambly: the family of Albert Provost, three marriages and fourteen children (1770-1813)
properties.description: The registers of Saint-Joseph de Chambly make it possible to rebuild Étienne's family. His father Albert, son of Gabriel Provost and Marie-Anne Bourassa, married Marie-Louise Paquet on January 29, 1770; their children were Marie-Louise (1771, died 1773), Isabelle (1773), Albert (1774), Joseph (1776), Charles (1778), Marie-Angélique (1779), Pierre (1781) and François-Marie (1782, died 1784). He then married Magdeleine Lebeau on June 2, 1783, and Marie-Anne Mainard on January 25, 1785. From this last marriage came Étienne (1785), Toussaint (1787), Julien (1789), Antoine (1790), Raphaël (1791) and François (1792), the last two dying as infants. Albert was buried on March 5, 1796. His younger brothers stayed home: Toussaint married Émilie Robert in 1806 and Julien married Josephte Fréchette in 1813, when Étienne had probably already left for the West.
properties.sources: Drouin, Quebec, Canada, Vital and Church Records (Drouin Collection), 1621-1968, Saint-Joseph parish, Chambly (Ancestry, accessed November 20, 2026) ; Ancestry tree “Étienne Provost (1785-1850) – Atlas Provost” (O. J. Caron, 2026)
properties.note: Same registers as L01; the point is offset from the church so as not to hide it. The parents of Marie-Louise Paquet and Magdeleine Lebeau, and each wife's death date, remain to be found.

properties.nom: St. Louis: Mary Rose Provost marries James A. H. Pillsbury (1857-1880)
properties.description: On May 27, 1857, Mary Rose, Étienne's daughter, married James A. H. Pillsbury, born about 1827 in New Hampshire, at the Cathedral before Rev. S. A. Paris; the Missouri Republican announced the marriage of “Miss Mary R. Provat.” The 1860 census finds them in St. Louis Ward 3: he is a grocer; with them live their daughter Mary Frances, born about 1860, and a twelve-year-old Celestine Pillsbury whose relationship is unknown. A son, Etienne A., was born about 1862, named after his grandfather. In 1880 James, a retired broker, and his family lived at 900 Third Street. Etienne A. married Elizabeth Amplemen in December 1883. James died on November 18, 1889, aged 62, at their home at 901 South Second Street, a short walk from the old Provost house at Lombard and Second; his funeral was held at Annunciation Church.
properties.sources: Recensements des États-Unis de 1860 (St. Louis Ward 3) et de 1880 (Saint-Louis), Ancestry ; Missouri Republican, 1er juin 1857 ; St. Louis Republic, 25 décembre 1883 ; St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 19 novembre 1889 et 31 août 1913 ; arbre Ancestry « Étienne Provost (1785-1850) – Atlas Provost » ; presse : Newspapers.com (abonnement de l'auteur), consulté le 20 novembre 2026
properties.note: Hypothetical point: Ward 3 in 1860 and 900 Third Street are placed in old St. Louis near the river, without precise geocoding.

presse.legende: Missouri Republican, 1er juin 1857 : mariage de James A. H. Pillsbury et de « Miss Mary R. Provat »
St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 19 novembre 1889 : mort de James A. Pillsbury

properties.nom: St. Louis: the Grimm descendants, from 14th Street to Virginia Avenue (1881-1913)
properties.description: About 1881 Mary Frances Pillsbury, Étienne's granddaughter, married Charles G. Grimm, born about 1858 in Missouri, a brewery cashier in 1910. The couple had five children in the censuses: Mary E. (c. 1885), Clara E. (c. 1888), Margaret M. A. (c. 1894), Ferdinand (c. 1898) and Agnes Maria (1900). In 1900 they lived at 1322 14th Street; in 1910 at 4231 Virginia Avenue in south St. Louis. The widowed Mary Rose lived with them and died in 1913 nearby, at 4231 South 37th Street (L43). The 1913 death notice names her grandchildren: Sister Mary of the Visitation, Sister Lucy of the Good Shepherd Convent, Margaret, Ferdinand and Agnes Grimm. Her son Etienne A. Pillsbury died in St. Louis on October 6, 1927, leaving two sons, Charles and Philip Pillsbury.
properties.sources: Recensements des États-Unis de 1900 et de 1910 (Saint-Louis), Ancestry ; St. Louis Star and Times, 10 août 1913, p. 17 ; St. Louis Globe-Democrat, 9 août 1913 ; St. Louis Post-Dispatch, 7 octobre 1927 ; arbre Ancestry « Étienne Provost (1785-1850) – Atlas Provost » ; presse : Newspapers.com (abonnement de l'auteur), consulté le 20 novembre 2026
properties.note: Point at 4231 Virginia Avenue (Dutchtown), approximate. The 1900 14th Street address is not geocoded.

properties.nom: Carondelet: the Delor de Tréget, family of Provost's wife's mother (1767-1837)
properties.description: Mary Rose Provost's grandmother was Madeleine Delor. She was the daughter of Clément Delor de Tréget, “former officer in the service of the Most Christian King,” a native of Cahors who left Sainte-Geneviève in 1767 to found, on the Mississippi south of St. Louis, the village later called Carondelet, or Vide-Poche, and of Catherine Marin. On December 31, 1781, in St. Louis, Madeleine first married François Cailhol of Marseille. She later became the wife of Lambert Salé dit Lajoie, with whom she had at least Marie-Gertrude (1794), Caroline, Clément and Marie-Rose, the future Mrs. Provost. She was buried in St. Louis on February 3, 1837, “aged 78.” In 1913 her name resurfaced, as “Madelin Delor,” on the death certificate of her great-granddaughter, as that of Mary Rose's mother.
properties.sources: Drouin, U.S., French Catholic Church Records (Drouin Collection), 1695-1954, Saint-Louis (vieille cathédrale) : mariage Cailhol – Delor, 31 décembre 1781 (registre des mariages 1781-1828, image 3) ; mariage Provost – Lambert, 4 août 1829 ; sépulture de « Mme Lambert Lajoie », 3 février 1837 (sépultures 1832-1847, image 27), Ancestry, lus le 20 novembre 2026 ; Missouri, U.S., Compiled Marriages, 1754-1850 ; Missouri State Board of Health, certificat de décès n° 27938 (1913) ; Chemins de la francophonie, « Carondelet, a Fathers' Rendez-vous » (en ligne)
properties.note: Point at the heart of old Carondelet. Madeleine's birth date is uncertain: 78 at burial would give about 1759, while online family trees give August 4, 1766, at Sainte-Geneviève, without a cited source. The date of her marriage to Lambert Salé and what became of François Cailhol remain to be found.

properties.nom: Taos: the capture of María Rosa Villalpando, Mary Rose's great-grandmother (1760)
properties.description: On August 4, 1760, Comanches attacked Pablo Villalpando's estancia near Taos, New Mexico, killed the defenders and carried off some fifty women and children. Among them was María Rosa Villalpando, whose young son escaped the raid. Traded to the Pawnees, she met the trader Jean Salé dit Lajoie, who took her to St. Louis with their son Lambert, born in 1768; they married there in 1770. Lambert was the father of Marie-Rose, Étienne Provost's wife: Mary Rose Provost was thus the great-granddaughter of the Taos captive. María Rosa died in St. Louis in July 1830; the Old Cathedral register records her burial on July 28, “wife of Jean Salé,” aged, it says, one hundred and four. Provost had married her granddaughter a year earlier. Another grandson, Antoine Leroux, son of Hélène Salé, became a famous guide of the Southwest and settled in Taos.
properties.sources: Tykal, Jack B. (1990), « Taos to St. Louis: The Journey of Maria Rosa Villalpando », New Mexico Historical Review, 65 (2), p. 162-167 ; Brooks, James F. (2002), Captives and Cousins, Chapel Hill, University of North Carolina Press ; Wikipédia, « Maria Rosa Villalpando » (consulté le 20 novembre 2026) ; New Mexico Historic Women, « Maria Rosa Villapando » (en ligne) ; Drouin, U.S., French Catholic Church Records (Drouin Collection), 1695-1954, Saint-Louis (vieille cathédrale), sépultures 1781-1832, acte du 28 juillet 1830 (image 168) ; mariage Provost – Lambert, 4 août 1829 ; Missouri, U.S., Compiled Marriages, 1754-1850 (Hélène Salé × Benjamin Leroux, 7 janvier 1792)
properties.note: Genealogical entry outside Étienne's life, like L02. Point at Ranchos de Taos. The age of 104 in the register is exaggerated: historians place her birth around 1738. Jack B. Tykal, Provost's biographer, also wrote the standard study of María Rosa Villalpando. Antoine Leroux was thus a first cousin of Provost's wife.

properties.nom: St. Louis: Provost stands surety for the estate of his father-in-law Lambert Salé dit Lajoie (February 22, 1837)
properties.description: On February 22, 1837, before the St. Louis County Court, Clément Sallé dit Lajoie, Marie-Rose's brother, becomes administrator "de bonis non with the will annexed" of the estate of his father, Lambert Sallé dit Lajoie, who died in 1834. He is bound for $1,000 to the State of Missouri, with two sureties: Étienne Provost ("Etienne Provos"), his brother-in-law, and John B. Sarpy, a partner in Pierre Chouteau Jr. & Co., Provost's employer. Clément signs; Provost, who could not write, makes his cross between "his" and "mark", as on his 1829 marriage record. The bond is recorded on March 1, 1837, by clerk Henry Chouteau. "De bonis non" means administering the goods left unsettled when the first executor can no longer act: the widow, Madeleine Delor, had been buried nineteen days earlier, on February 3 (L70). A few weeks later Provost leaves again for the mountains with the company caravan (L31).
properties.sources: Administrator's bond of Clément Sallé alias Lajoie, estate of Lambert Sallé dit Lajoie, with Étienne Provos and John B. Sarpy as sureties, St. Louis, February 22, 1837, recorded March 1, 1837 (Henry Chouteau, clerk), St. Louis County Court; Missouri, U.S., Wills and Probate Records, estate of Lambert Salle, St. Louis (file no. 1153); document supplied by the atlas author
properties.note: Point at the St. Louis courthouse (site of today's Old Courthouse, Fourth and Market streets). The printed form has "Execut[rix]" struck out, pointing to a previous executor, probably the widow; that Madeleine Delor was her husband's executrix remains an inference to check against Lambert's will (not read). The bond confirms Provost as Clément's brother-in-law, shows the American Fur Company backing his family affairs, and places him in St. Louis at the end of winter 1837.

properties.nom: St. Louis: the house at the corner of Lombard and Second streets (1839-1918)
properties.description: The house where Étienne Provost died on July 3, 1850, stood “on the corner of Lombard and Second streets,” in Frenchtown south of the old town. His will of April 1, 1839 leaves Marie-Rose this lot “on the Corner of Lombard and Second Streets,” fifty feet on Second by 150 on Lombard, “it being the same on which I now reside”; the 1850 inventory specifies block 49, bounded west by Papin and south by Pilcher, and the city valued the house at $1,100. The 1843 tax list places him at the east end of city block 49, on the south side of Lombard; the 1840-1845 directories list an “H. N. Provost,” grocer, at the southwest corner of Second and Lombard; Hutawa's 1850 plan shows block 49 at that exact corner, Palmatary's great view (c. 1857-1858) draws a three-story house at the corner of Lombard and Second, and the bird's-eye Pictorial St. Louis (1875, plate 3) draws two gabled two-story houses and a tree-lined yard along Lombard. After the 1866 numbering the corner house became 901 South Second Street, and the family stayed there until at least 1889: Étienne's granddaughter Mary Frances Grimm lost a child there in 1882, Maskow relatives lived there in 1884 and 1888, and Mary Rose's husband James A. H. Pillsbury died there in 1889. The 1908 Sanborn map shows a two-story brick building with a store on the ground floor; it was still occupied in 1916. On April 26, 1918, the St. Louis Republic lists a demolition permit: “Jos. Kelly, 901-05 South Second, wreck; $1,000.” The house was torn down in the spring of 1918. In 2015 the corner is an empty lot under the railway viaduct; the neighbouring building at 907, built between 1875 and 1908 (J. H. Buel's japanning shop in 1908-1910), still stands (author's photographs, August 17, 2015). In August 2016, street repairs exposed, under the asphalt of Lombard Street between Second and Fourth, alongside the lot, a pavement of creosoted sweet-gum blocks laid in the late nineteenth century, quickly covered over again (St. Louis Post-Dispatch, September 4, 2016). The corner is now crossed by the MacArthur Bridge railway approach, in the Chouteau's Landing district.

properties.nom: Carignan, chemin Salaberry: Étienne Provost's birthplace (probable site), on the land conceded to Gabriel Provost in 1745
properties.description: The inventory drawn up on July 15, 1783 by the notary Antoine Grisé, after the death of Marie-Louise Paquet, describes the farm of Albert Provost, Étienne's father: “a lot three arpents wide by forty-six [reading to be confirmed] deep, in the barony of Longueuil, on the Petite rivière de Montréal, with a squared-log house thirty feet by twenty-eight, well habitable, two barns also in good order, and a stable fifteen feet by eleven.” The Petite rivière de Montréal is today's rivière L'Acadie, which flows into the Chambly basin. Albert raised the children of his first marriage there (Élisabeth, Joseph, Charles, Pierre, François), with two horses, two mares and their foals, seventeen pigs and hens. In all likelihood Étienne was born there in December 1785, of Albert's third marriage to Marie-Anne Mainard; the family had its children baptized at Chambly.
properties.sources: Inventaire des biens de la communauté d'Albert Provost et de Marie-Louise Paquet, 15 juillet 1783, greffe d'Antoine Grisé dit Villefranche, acte no 2493, BAnQ CN601,S189, microfilm FamilySearch 1420479 (DGS 008326749), images 2702-2712 ; concession no 2036 du 15 juin 1781 (Albert « demeurant à Chambly ») ; Bouchette, Joseph (1815), Topographical Map of the Province of Lower Canada, David Rumsey Map Collection
properties.note: The Provost family farm, conceded on 5 October 1745 by the Baroness of Longueuil to Gabriel Provost, Étienne's grandfather (notary Gervais Hodiesne), according to the declaration made by Julien Provost's widow for the papier-terrier of the Barony (c. 1847): 3 arpents 2 feet wide by 29 to 31 arpents deep, 91 arpents, on the Petite rivière de Montréal, “with a house, barn and other buildings.” It is lot no. 1374 in the 1861 abridged cadastre (“Veuve Julien Provost”), lots 190-191 on the 1868 plan, and today lots 2 601 544, 2 601 646 and 2 601 647 in Carignan; Albert lived there in 1783 (log house, 30 × 28 feet); Étienne was very probably born there in 1785. Neighbours: the Paquets (family of Marie-Louise Paquet), the Quintins and, a few farms away, the Lamoureux (1794 arbitration); Moïse Lamoureux, later Aubry's employer in St. Louis, grew up on lot no. 1381, about 900 m south-west (Aubry atlas). See the Chambly tab in the reading room. Site of the house: at the front of the farm, between the L'Acadie River (about 45.4155 N, 73.3677 W) and chemin Salaberry (about 45.4129 N, 73.3628 W), on current lot 2 601 544; the point is placed on chemin Salaberry. The exact position of the house within this front is not known. Houses standing today on the front of the farm: no. 4760 (one-and-a-half-storey farmhouse, construction date not published, on the north-east limit), no. 4781 (1990), no. 4824 (1976); none is recognized as old by the MRC built-heritage inventory (2025). Evidence for the identification: see the section on what is certain and what is probable in the Chambly tab. properties.nom: La Petite-Cadie (L'Acadie): the two lots granted to Albert Provost (June 15, 1781)
properties.description: On June 15, 1781, before the Chambly notary Antoine Grisé dit Villefranche, “messire Joseph Fleury, écuyer, sieur Deschambault, in the name of and as guardian of the baroness of Longueuil, his granddaughter,” granted to “Albert Proveau, living at Chambly” two lots three arpents wide by thirty deep in the seigneury of Longueuil, “à la petite Cadie,” “fronting on the rivière de Montréal, at the back on ungranted land”; the first adjoined Étienne Dumas on one side and Joseph Tremblay on the other, the second adjoined Dumas and ungranted land. Rent: two sols cens, one sol per arpent and half a minot of wheat per twenty arpents, due at Martinmas. In 1783 both lots were still “all standing timber.” La Petite-Cadie was the settlement founded on the rivière L'Acadie by deported Acadians who arrived in 1768, around today's village of L'Acadie, parish of Sainte-Marguerite-de-Blairfindie from 1784.

The grantor, Joseph Fleury Deschambault, trustee of the barony, was replaced that same year by David Alexander Grant.

properties.nom: Michilimackinac: Étienne Provost hired as a voyageur for the « Southern Dependencies » (1805)
properties.description: On 25 January 1805, in Montreal, before notary Jonathan A. Gray, « Etienne Provost » of the parish of L'Acadie signed on for one year with Parker, Gerrard, Ogilvy & Co. as a « milieu » (middle paddler) and winterer, bound for Michilimackinac and the « Dépendances du Sud ». He was 19. Wages: 500 livres, with advances of 8 piastres at signing and 8 at departure, plus « an ordinary double outfit ». The « Southern Dependencies » were the posts south-west of Michilimackinac: Green Bay, the Fox and Wisconsin rivers, Prairie du Chien and the upper Mississippi — the road to St. Louis. It is the earliest known document of his life as a voyageur.

properties.nom: Prairie du Chien: gateway to the Mississippi on the road to St. Louis (1805-1814, hypothesis)
properties.description: At the mouth of the Wisconsin, Prairie du Chien was the great meeting place of Michilimackinac traders heading down to St. Louis. Hired in 1805 for the « Southern Dependencies », Provost must have passed through. No document yet places him between 1805 and 1814, when he left St. Louis with Joseph Philibert.
